title: The 10 issues I see when I watch maths lessons... and what we can do about it
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton draws on visits to roughly two schools a week and thousands of observed lessons to list the ten problems he sees most often in maths classrooms, however different the schools are. The list follows the lesson in order: students who are quiet but not actually listening, unreliable checks for understanding, a one-size response to those checks, a Do Now that becomes dead time, and missing prerequisite knowledge. It continues through muddled I Dos and We Dos, a drop in effort at the start of independent practice, a lack of problem-solving for most students, and forgetting. Each issue is paired with a proposed fix such as listening checks, mass participation, atomisation, separating the I Do from the We Do, and scheduled retrieval. He frames the list as a self-audit, asking which issues the reader has nailed and how they know. The piece is partly a signpost to his free write-ups and paid CPD workshops, but the diagnostic list itself is a useful map of common lesson weaknesses.
points: Quiet, attentive-looking students are often not listening at all, which is why Barton proposes regular checks for listening rather than trusting appearances.
Relying on volunteers or cold calling gives a single, unrepresentative data point, so mass participation is needed for reliable checks for understanding.
Teachers often respond identically whatever the data shows, wasting time on secure concepts and starving the shaky ones.
Barton argues that gaps in prerequisite knowledge should be found and fixed by atomising the new idea before the I Do, not discovered mid-explanation.
Problem-solving is rarely offered beyond top sets, and retrieval is rarely scheduled, so students both miss out on challenge and lose what they once knew.
quotes: In almost every lesson I visit, I see examples of students not listening to instructions, explanations, or their peers' responses. Sometimes, this lack of attention is visible - students talk to each other while the teacher is talking.

The issue here is that we only get a single data point, and we are then forced to make decisions about the understanding of the rest of the class based on such a small, often unrepresentative, sample.

I often see teachers respond the same way regardless of what their students' data shows them. This leads to a misallocation of time, where concepts that students are secure on are laboured over, leaving little time for those concepts where students need teacher support.

I regularly see Do Nows that last 15 or 20 minutes, and at the end of it, many students have learned very little as they have been busy tricking - waiting for the teacher to go through the answers, so they can fill them in and proudly adorn their work with lovely green ticks.

The second mistake is building in checks for that prerequisite knowledge whilst simultaneously presenting the new idea - so checking for understanding during an I Do. This often leads to I Dos veering off course as the teachers find they have to address a surprising gap in knowledge.

I go through entire days watching lessons without seeing any student answer any question beyond basic consolidation. When I do see students do something more sophisticated with a procedure, it tends to be students in top sets or the one or two high-flyers who finish a piece of work early.

I often flick through books and see evidence of students understanding a concept in the moment, only to have seemingly forgotten it completely a few weeks later when they need it. This is frustrating for students and teachers alike.
